Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity this afternoon to speak to Bill C-204. If I appear to be out of breath it is because I got here at the last minute to join in the debate, but I did want to take a few minutes to express support for Bill C-204 introduced by the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald).

I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for the effort she is putting into this Bill. I said this to the Hon. Member before, but I know she has, shall I say, much less tolerance for smokers than perhaps some other people do. She has a religious fervour of sorts for this measure she is proposing and I congratulate her for that. I know there are several of us who do not smoke and have smoke puffed in our face quite often. Sometimes, because we are in elected office, we do not dare say anything, but we should on occasion. I know that is not the case with the Hon. Member, so I am told by several people. I will not describe the kinds of meetings where she has told people to butt out, but I am sure some of her colleagues could attest to the fact there have been such occasions. At least so I have heard.
The important point is that we often hear on radio commercials dealing with this subject. I was listening to CKO this morning and there was a commercial from Health and Welfare Canada. It was very well done. It said that if someone was burning trash in their backyard and polluting everyone else, the municipal authorities would fine them. That is quite true in a number of localities. If someone was poisoning the air for someone else we would not put up with it. Yet at the same time many people are smoking and causing that kind of harm to themselves and others around them. The interesting point is that the commercial ends by saying "It is enough to take your breath away". Obviously it is, literally speaking.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I quit smoking myself about fifteen years ago and I can assure you that the presence of smoke around us is becoming ever more difficult to accept despite the fact that some of us do tolerate it, even though we should not. Statistics make it obvious that similar efforts must be made to reduce the number of opportunities people have to smoke, not only to protect their own health but, more important still, the health of people around them.

There are some diseases which are almost totally and exclusively caused by the fact that people smoke. That is very unfortunate. On the other hand, some people tell us that Governments need the revenue which the tax on cigarette tobacco produces. With those who subscribe to that theory I have to disagree profoundly. First, the health costs associated with the diseases caused by smoking far exceed any revenue the Government could ever hope to generate from the tobacco tax. That has been proven so many times that we need not go into it now in further detail. The other fact is that there is really no price to be put on good health. All of us know, particularly those of us who have had family members get sick, or have been sick ourselves, that we do not know how well we are until we are sick. Then we know just how precious health is. Unfortunately, too many people who smoke do not always give this fact the kind of attention they should.
February 12, 1987

I have a few small concerns about the Bill. They do not in any way take away from my intention of supporting its general thrust. But I bring to the attention of the House that in my view there should be some sort of exception clauses to make it more realistic and suitable to circumstances. Let us say we are talking about a building with a designated smoking room. Perhaps because of the size of certain buildings there should be some exceptions. I am thinking that it would not be necessary to have a separate smoking area for two people working in an airplane hangar or something like that. There has to be some kind of practical adjustment to make the Bill a little more functional. I want to caution Members of the House that it may require some mild amendments like that, friendly amendments, but that does not take away from the fact that I intend to support the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would rather not use up all the time allocated to me today. One of the reasons is that I hope this Bill will be given second reading and sent to a parliamentary committee so that we might make a detailed study and propose certain amendments which might be necessary. In any event, I know other Members intend to express their views on this measure. Therefore I yield the floor to other Members who, I am sure, will also make an important contribution to this debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, cigarette smoking is emerging as a major public health concern for many Canadians probably because smoking can cause illness and shorten our life expectancy and because it is a habit that is difficult to break and becomes addictive. The public is also increasingly aware of the fact that smoking is not only bad for smokers. The latest research has shown that smoke produced by others, known as sidestream or secondary smoke, may be the cause of low birth weight and fetal injury. It can also cause respiratory illness in children and lung cancer in subjects exposed to sidestream smoke for long periods, for instance in the home or at work. As a result of this growing awareness of the effects of smoking, the public wants action to be taken on several issues, including cigarette advertising and exposure to sidestream smoke in public vehicles and at work.
The Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) is to be commended for presenting a Bill whose purpose is to reduce tobacco consumption and protect the public from involuntary exposure to sidestream smoke. I support the spirit and the intent of the Bill, and I would like to start with a few comments on tobacco advertising.
The Association for Non-Smokers' Rights has documented numerous violations of the voluntary code that manufacturers of tobacco products have agreed to apply to advertising and promotion, including advertising tobacco products on billboards and in stores within less than 200 metres of school property.
In 1986, the "Tempo" cigarette ad campaign aroused public concern. In my view, the campaign was clearly directed at
Non-Smokers' Health Act
recruiting new smokers among Canadian youth, thus violating the voluntary advertising code. The new 15-cigarette Export A pack has also been cause for concern, since the cheaper price makes this product more accessible to young Canadians. Unfortunately, in a declining tobacco market we can expect an increasing number of these questionable advertising and promotion campaigns.
For some time there has been concern that a product as dangerous as tobacco should a subject of promotion and advertizing campaigns, especially since the ad associate tobacco with a healthy, exciting and glamorous lifestyle, make tobacco products more attractive to young people and generally legitimize tobacco use. In fact, a number of Canadian magazines and newspapers, including the Kingston Whig-Standard, the Brockville Recorder and Times, the Globe and Mail and the Toronto Star, are now refusing to accept tobacco advertising because they believe it is unethical to advertise a product that is so clearly hazardous and addictive, and they are to be commended for doing so.
Although voluntary commitments by the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers Council have been successful in limiting tobacco advertising to a certain extent and have also included the printing of health warnings on cigarette packs and reducing tar and carbon monoxide levels produced by cigarettes, the violations of the Code prove that the self-regulating approach is not ideal. Without provisions for enforcement, manufacturers are under no obligation whatsoever to observe this Code.
The federal Government has met with representatives of the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers Council with a view to taking stronger action on tobacco advertising and promotion. Of special concern are the issues of lifestyle advertising and promotion aimed at teenagers and adults, the effectiveness of current health warnings, and the effectiveness of current compliance procedures. A number of options are being considered for restricting tobacco advertising, and I am very sure, Mr. Speaker, that this Government will be introducing further measures in the near future.
Another major point is involuntary exposure to cigarette smoke. I think we should realize that more and more, Canadians are demanding smoke-free areas, especially at work, in public vehicles and other public places such as restaurants, hospitals and retail stores.
A good many public and private sector initiatives designed to establish smoke-free areas have made it possible to protect the Canadian public against the hazards of involuntary contact with the tobacco smoke of other people. We should all commend the efforts of Canadians who have taken such initiatives.
As to smoking on public transport systems, several major bus transport companies, including Greyhound, Gray Coach, Voyageur, Canadian Coach and Pacific Coach, now offer services reserved for non-smokers only on many routes. As well, most major cities have banned smoking on municipal

February 12, 1987
Non-Smokers' Health Act
buses. Carriers such as Air Maritime, NorOntair, Time Air and Air Nova have flights for non-smokers and, for a few months now, most Air Canada Rapidair flights within the Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal triangle have been reserved for nonsmokers. Last month, in response to public pressure, VIA Rail management decided to run cars for non-smokers on all but five of their routes, and all their coaches also have seats reserved for non-smokers. Better still, recently the Minister of Transport announced a proposed regulation to ban smoking on Canadian aircraft on domestic and transborder flights of two hours or less. Mr. Speaker, this measure marks another decisive phase in a series of concerted efforts to protect the travelling public against the hazards of involuntary exposure to sidestream smoke.
More and more employers are establishing policies which restrict smoking in the workplace. For example, Boeing, the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia and a variety of other companies have adopted as their goal a smoke-free workplace and are moving in that direction. Bata Industries Limited has already entirely banned smoking on the job. Municipalities such as the City of Ottawa are banning smoking at work stations and are working toward a complete ban on smoking in the workplace.
According to the Institute for Occupational Smoking Policy at the University of Seattle, employers who allow smoking in the workplace have much higher costs related to employee absenteeism, property damage and maintenance. Employees who smoke spend 6 per cent of their working hours on this ritual. Obviously, every employee who does not smoke on the job is a definite asset to the employer. Banning smoking from the workplace has other advantages as well. Some employers have observed that in addition to protecting their employees against the hazards of tobacco smoke and saving on maintenance costs, the restrictions imposed on smokers at work greatly improved employee morale.
Mr. Speaker, most major cities in Canada impose smoking restrictions in other public areas and gradually pass ever stricter by-laws in this respect.
This year Quebec enacted legislation to restrict smoking in various public places. It is a first at the provincial level. The Quebec legislation has two major aspects. First, smoking is banned or restricted to certain designated areas in government offices, hospitals, schools, public transit vehicles, and many other public buildings. Second, municipalities are authorized to pass additional smoking by-laws applicable to places under their jurisdiction. Quite a few municipal councils have taken this opportunity to adopt even stricter regulations which were not covered under the earlier provisions so as to restrict smoking in public areas, particularly places of work.
The federal administration has also made a special effort to designate rooms where smoking is prohibited in its offices. Considering that employee exposure to the tobacco smoke of others is not in keeping with the over-all objective, which is to maintain a healthy working climate, and that employees want to have much stiffer restrictions in that respect, a number of
Departments have decided to restrict smoking in their offices. Among others I might mention the Office of the Auditor General, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, the Department of National Health and Welfare, Statistics Canada, the National Research Council, the National Library Catalogue Division, and the Public Service Commission. In addition, the National Joint Council, an employer-union organization, is now considering various ways to strengthen the policy governing the use of tobacco in federal workplaces. For example, Mr. Speaker, last week Petro-Canada management announced smoking restrictions in their offices and facilities. Thus the federal administration is making an effort to promote smoke-free workplaces and leading the way for employers who have not yet implemented this kind of policy.
Although the federal Government has already established policies and programs aimed at restricting tobacco use, we can expect to see much more comprehensive measures to protect the public against exposure to the smoke of others, as well as restrictions concerning current tobacco marketing practices.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this afternoon to say two things. First, I fully support Bill C-204 and I commend the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for daring to be the first elected representative in the history of this place to deal with a danger which has affected us throughout the history of Parliament. Second, let me assure my esteemed colleague and true friend in connection with this and other causes we share that I do not enter this debate as a result of her friendly but forceful persuasion. I support this Bill because of long, bitter and sometimes hilarious experience in the more than a quarter of a century it has taken me to realize that smoking can indeed be dangerous to one's health.
It will come as no staggering surprise to anyone who knows me that I enjoy a pipe. Hon. Members rarely see me without a pipe, unlit but always at hand, even in this Chamber, as a kind of crutch, a prop, or, as the late, great Prime Minister John Diefenbaker used to kid me, "It gives you that something, that sense of sobriety which isn't always present in the journalistic community". The former Right Hon. Member for Prince Albert was correct way back then.
As a Member of this House, I admit that the pipe may provide an image, though not for the reasons Mr. Diefenbaker mentioned. Indeed, as the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood notes with horror at the commencement of every Standing and Special Parliamentary Committee on which we have participated, my pipe sits in an ashtray at the Chairperson's place and invariably she remarks, "You're not going to light that, are you, Mr. Chairman?" The answer has always been no and the answer here, Lynn, is also no.
I guess this is as good a time as any to recount an experience I had in a previous workplace, an experience which seemed very funny at the time to the distinguished person involved but
February 12, 1987

which almost proved to be extremely hazardous to me. The people involved in this episode were my friend, Bob Hull, former Ottawa Bureau Chief of the Windsor Star, myself, then President of the Parliamentary Press Gallery and Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II. The workplace on this occasion in 1973 was Government House. The occasion was an official reception for the media in honour of Her Majesty given by Governor General Roland Michener in the tent room at Rideau Hall.
As executives of the Press Gallery, Mr. Hull and I were among the first to be presented to the Queen and His Excellency and then we were ushered into the elaborately decorated tent room for drinks and chatter until the Royal Party joined us. Bob Hull and I were advised to station ourselves right next to the entrance to the tent room in order to welcome Her Majesty and escort her informally through the growing throng of media people.
Both Bob Hull and I were pipe smokers and, as we lit up and a waiter handed us our drinks, Bob only had time to get out the question, "Now that we've gone through the receiving line and we're all here informally, are we allowed to smoke and drink in front of the Queen? I mean, what do we do if she-" and she did, Mr. Speaker.
Out of the corner of my eye, I was aware that an elegant, diminutive lady, all by herself, was approaching the two of us. Three things happened all at once. I stiffened and whispered to Bob, "Stash it, she's here". My friend found a nearby shelf with an ashtray and was able to dispose of his pipe and his drink in time to fold his hands neatly and say hello to Her Majesty. I was not so lucky. I plunged my pipe into my coat pocket and whipped back my right arm with the drink in my hand and said, without looking, "Here, somebody please take this". Not exactly composed, I then proceeded to join in the conversation with Her Majesty. Suddenly she started to laugh. I know that the British and especially the Royal family have a great sense of humour but I did not recall having said anything that funny or looking particularly funny. And then I smelled it. By now the Queen was in near hysterics as aides materialized out of nowhere asking her if something was wrong. Queen Elizabeth could only get out, through her uncontrollable giggling, "No, not with me, but sir," she said to me, "will you please take that infernal pipe out of your pocket or you'll burn the whole place down". I stabbed my finger into the smouldering pipe bowl, and as the ever-present aide rushed up with a damp napkin to stifle the rising column of smoke, the Queen continued, "And now, look who you just handed your drink to". There was His Excellency, Governor General Roland Michener, standing with two drinks, his and mine, muttering, "It's all right, Geoff, I'm just a supernumerary around here when Her Majesty is around. It's just part of the job".
So many millions of Canadians regard smoking as just part of the job. A number of colleagues from all sides of the House have presented detailed and valid reasons to persuade Canadians to change the way that smoking is considered to be just part of the job.
Non-Smokers' Health Act
The first charge that could be levelled at such a piece of legislation as Bill C-204 is that it tramples on the rights of individuals. In my view, this Bill is not interventionist and does not trample on the rights of individuals. The statistics fly in the face of any such argument. Statistics show that smoking is the greatest cause of preventable death. Smoking accounts for almost 20 per cent of Canadian deaths, killing more Canadians than alcohol, car accidents, violence, drugs, suicides and poisoning combined. Smoking kills 32,000 Canadians every year. Four million Canadians will die from the effects of tobacco products and each smoker will die, on average, eight years prematurely.
There is a growing awareness of the dangers of second-hand smoke. A recent Health and Welfare study found that one in five Canadians has a serious medical condition which is aggravated by second-hand smoke. Other Hon. Members have mentioned that those who have asthma, emphysema or heart disease, will substantiate that. Health and Welfare Canada also estimated that 1,050 non-smoking Canadians will die from lung cancer, perhaps one-half of them from second-hand smoke.
With regard to the economic costs of smoking, Health and Welfare Canada estimated that the cost associated with smoking is twice as high as the revenue from tobacco taxation. The Health and Welfare study pointed out that the economic costs of tobacco use in terms of mortality, disability, fire damage, direct hospitalization and physicians' fees is $7.12 billion versus $4.2 billion in economic revenue from the tobacco industry.
By debating this kind of legislation, we are not trampling on people's lives. We are trying to address the case of the majority. Two-thirds of Canadians do not smoke. We are only trying to minimize the effects of smoking on both smokers and non-smokers. I do not think any Canadian would object to that as long as the legislation allows those who wish to smoke to do so. No one is trying to remove that right from those individuals because we do live in a free society.
There is no question that passage of Bill C-204 and the proclamation of this law will be an immensely important signal to employers and to Canadians generally that an official new awareness has dawned concerning smoking in the workplace. The legislation will only be meaningful in the long run in the ways it is followed up in practice.
I wonder if the historic measure the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood is hoping to pass in the very near future will not have achieved its main purpose initially by being simply a clear signal, a symbol, a beacon, if you wish, that employers had better start recognizing the problem of the non-smoker. Sometimes it does not take the force of law to bring about that kind of change, at least in some areas. We have found a simple answer in the Standing Committee on Secretary of State. We simply removed all ashtrays permanently. People do not mind stepping out into the hall to light up. I do not notice fewer passengers flying the one or two-hour non-smoking Air Canada flights since Transport Canada

February 12, 1987
Adjournment Debate
brought in that regulation. Smoking on an aircraft has always been a crazy hazard anyway. Now I sense that folks are beginning to appreciate a smoke-free environment in the air.
In short, and in conclusion, the idea of a smoke-free environment is seeping into the minds of walking smoke stacks such as those we find in this very Chamber. Moments before entering the House I saw my colleague, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), sitting all alone in the huge, leather-chaired lobby of the Confederation Building puffing away on his cigarette. He had just decreed a no-smoking rule in his office and had to abide by it with his lonely vigil of the sixth floor of the Confederation Building. If my friend from Western Arctic can respect other's wishes in this workplace, anyone can.
Again, I commend the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood for presenting a basically sound Bill, one that I will be happy to support when this historic measure is brought to a vote.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS-WORKER'S PAY CHEQUES-REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION CONCERNING CERTAIN DEDUCTIONS MADE AT SOURCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday on February 6, 1987, I stated before the House my concern about the NDP's funding sources. In raising this issue in the House, I referred to a 123-page judgment of the Ontario Supreme Court, handed down on July 7, 1986 by Mr. Justice John White.
In his judgment, Judge White of the Ontario Supreme Court referred to representations that were made before the Court at the request of a teacher at a college in Haileybury, Mr. Mervyn Lavigne. Mr. Lavigne's employer was deducting from his salary the union dues payable by all college employees, in accordance with the Rand formula.
The Rand formula obliges employees who decline membership in the union to pay the same dues as union members. The complainant in this case, Mr. Lavigne, did not object to the Rand formula as such but, under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, he objected to the fact that part of his
dues was not used exclusively for union business but for other purposes, including, and that is what is at issue today, contributions to the NDP. Mr. Speaker, it is common knowledge that the NDP gets a significant part of its funds from the unions.
Mr. Lavigne and his counsel argued the case before the Ontario Supreme Court and were able to prove to the satisfaction of the judge that under our Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, unions could not use funds raised in this way from Canadian workers for purposes other than union business.
Mr. Speaker, considering that as a result of the decision by Judge White of the Supreme Court of Ontario, the NDP finds itself in a rather uneasy situation with respect to fund-raising, and also considering that this case will probably go to the highest court in the land, the Supreme Court of Canada, I want to ask today, on the floor of this House, that every Member of the NDP cease to use union funds contributed by Canadian workers to support their party's finances.
To be more specific, Mr. Speaker, I am not suggesting that the NDP pay back to the unions the funds they have in their treasury at this time, but I think party officials would be showing their good faith if they put in trust the funds derived from the contributions referred to in the decision by the Supreme Court of Ontario. These amounts should be held in trust, first to protect our workers, and second, to comply with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
If the leader of the socialist party, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), really wants to be honest and to maintain the reputation for clarity and credibility he wants for his Party, he should immediately explain his position and that of all his colleagues as concerns this illegal use of the money contributed by our workers. What will the socialist party do about this matter?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw a parallel between this issue and the fact that, when Canadians, and more particularly Quebecers, they put a deposit on an item which they plan to purchase later from a retail store, our laws require that this deposit be put in trust by the store, even if it is a national chain, to ensure that the consumer is protected. I would like to point out that the retailers comply with this legal requirement and respect Canadian consumers.
Will the socialist party, which, by its own definition, presents itself as a party devoted first and foremost to respect for the consumer, now have the honesty, the straightforwardness and the strength to comply with the ruling of Mr. Justice White of the Supreme Court of Ontario in the Lavigne case and to put the contributions of workers in a trust fund, and most important, not to receive additional amounts from this now contested source? We shall see in coming days what the members of the socialist party do to comply with this principle and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and to remedy this situation. You can be assured, Mr. Speaker, that if they refuse to clarify their poisition before the Canadian
February 12, 1987

people and this House, we shall draw the inevitable conclusions and propose appropriate action.

subtopic: REVENUE CANADA-WORD PROCESSING WORK. (B) DEPARTMENT'S SECURITY MEASURES
REVENUE CANADA-WORD PROCESSING WORK. (B) DEPARTMENT'S SECURITY MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising as a result of a question that I asked of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay). It concerned reports in the Winnipeg newspapers that Revenue Canada was considering an experiment in contracting out word processing work that, in the opinion of the employees of the Tax Data Centre in Winnipeg, was confidential in nature. They brought this to my attention and the attention of the media. I met with them on Friday, February 6, at which time I learned about the Department's plans to experiment with this contracting out.
Subsequent to some attention being paid to this issue in The Winnipeg Free Press, particularly, there were reports that the Department backed down on its plan to experiment with contracting out. I asked the Minister to confirm that this was the case, which he did. It is a case where, at least in part, one received the answer one was hoping for. In this case, the Department had second thoughts about this kind of experiment. The official reason given was because of the effect on employee morale and the obvious degree to which this experiment was upsetting current employees of Revenue Canada.
I agree with that sentiment. I was dismayed to see that Revenue Canada would not only consider contracting out this kind of work, but would even entertain the idea.
I also raised the question of enhanced security measures at Revenue Canada. It is well known as a result of recent events, including the recent incident in Toronto involving microfiche, that there has been concern about security at Revenue Canada. I do not fault the Government for its concern, but I understand the concern of employees that the new policy, which I understand has been implemented, involves checks on
Adjournment Debate
elements of their personal lives about which they obviously feel sensitive.
There is a question of widespread fingerprinting, credit checks, as well as background searches for criminal records and other histories. If these checks must be done, they should be carried out with a great deal of sensitivity, particularly when one considers that many of these employees have worked for Revenue Canada from 10 to 20 years or more. They are concerned that any information that might be gathered in the course of these reliability checks could in fact be used against them when seeking a promotion or other appointments.
It is when they are appointed or promoted to a new position that these checks will come into force. It would be ironic-and I think this is one of the things we are concerned about-if a reliable employee for 10 or 20 years did have something in their past which, according to the new security guidelines, made them a risk, when we already know from their work history they are not, their chances then for promotion or for continuing employment are put at risk. That should not be so because of something which obviously has not had an effect on their reliability and on their trustworthiness as employees. Therefore, I can certainly understand, in the kind of example I have given, about the kind of concern employees may have.
We should also be concerned, even if there is an element of necessity to it whenever Governments feel they have to go to these kinds of measures, which are unprecedented really, to tighten up security. It is certainly regrettable that these kinds of things even have to be thought about. I wonder if the Parliamentary Secretary, or whoever is responding for the Minister, might also indicate on behalf of the Government whether this is part of a larger plan to have this kind of reliability or security check done in all government Departments.
There was also some concern expressed by the Public Service Alliance local with which I met that this was the beginning of a larger plan to do this in all government Departments. If that is the case, what we are looking at is "Big Brother". I know it is 1987, but 1984 is still the symbol of that Orwellian world we all want to avoid.
I would think it would be a Conservative Government, most of all, those who have raised concerns in the past about big Governments and Governments knowing everything there is to know about people, which ought to be more sensitive than perhaps previous Liberal Governments about that kind of information gathering, about widespread fingerprinting and about the kinds of things about which I think the Public Service Alliance people are so rightly concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: REVENUE CANADA-WORD PROCESSING WORK. (B) DEPARTMENT'S SECURITY MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his comments. I am sure he knows, as I do, that the Minister takes his comments very seriously. The Hon. Member raised two questions during Question Period on

February 12, 1987
Adjournment Debate
February 11. I will deal with the first question which concerned the proposal by Revenue Canada to review the feasibility of contracting out some word processing functions. The Hon. Member expressed concern that sensitive and confidential taxpayer information would be placed in jeopardy. First, as stated by the Minister, and referred to by the Hon. Member, as a result of further internal review and departmental investigation, the Department is not proceeding with the pilot projects. Second, no plans would have proceeded unless it could be assured that security of taxpayer information is maintained.
In his supplementary, the Hon. Member expressed concern about the Department's change in personnel security screening procedures which include fingerprinting, criminal record checks and credit checks. Revenue Canada has not departed from the government security policy. On the contrary, Revenue Canada fully supports the Government's policy, which was issued in June of 1986. It was the first Department to implement this new policy concerning personnel screening.
The purpose of the Treasury Board policy is to prescribe a security system for the Government of Canada which will effectively protect classified information and other assets sensitive to the national interests from unauthorized disclosure, destruction, removal, modification, or interruption. The policy is also intended to prescribe safeguards for other valuable assets and sensitive information such as tax returns. This is particularly important to Revenue Canada as its declaration of taxpayers' rights states that taxpayers: " have a special right that personal and financial information you provide to National Revenue Taxation will be used only for purposes allowed by law".
Because of the importance of confidentiality concerning taxpayer information, Revenue Canada decided to implement the new policy at an early date. This early implementation did follow consultation between Treasury Board and all Departments and between Taxation and the taxation component of the Public Service Alliance of Canada. Taxation employees
were then provided with information concerning the personnel screening part of the Government's security policy.
This program requires all candidates appointed from outside the Department, as well as current employees, when they are promoted, transferred, seconded or assigned positions for more than six months, to be subject to a basic or an enhanced reliability check. This screening program does not apply to employees in their current jobs.
A basic reliability check includes verification of personal data, educational and professional qualifications, and employment, as well as a name check of criminal records. An enhanced reliability check, valid for five years, requires a credit check and a fingerprint check in addition to the elements of a basic reliability check. The type of reliability check or security clearance required for a given position is based upon the level of sensitive information to which the position provides access, and the degree of that access as determined by departmental management. Any information obtained through this process is kept in the strictest confidence by the Department's security directorate.
It should be clear that this policy is not intended to be unfair to any employee. If a reliability check contains any adverse information, the employee will be given an opportunity to explain. If employees are denied an appointment as a result of a reliability check, they may use the current grievance process. A fair balance will be struck between the need to assure the Canadian public that their confidential tax information is protected by loyal and trustworthy staff and the desire to recognize the rights of employees.
